                                       PROJECT NO. 58000

 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                                §      PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                            §
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                          §                    OF TEXAS
 IN THE ERCOT REGION                                 §



                             CITY OF HOUSTON’S COMMENTS

        The City of Houston (Houston) submits the following comments on the Public Utility

Commission (Commission or PUC) Staff’s proposed amendments to §25.192 relating to

Transmission Rates and §25.193 relating to Distribution Service Provider Transmission Cost

Recovery Factors (TCRF) and new §25.252 relating to Large Load Customer Tariffs. Houston

appreciates the opportunity to provide the Commission with its comments.


                                     SPECIFIC COMMENTS

§25.192 Transmission Service Rates

        Houston supports the rule’s proposed 12CP demand allocation methodology. The four

summer months coincident peak (4CP) demand allocation methodology for allocating the Electric

Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) wholesale transmission cost of service (TCOS) has been

used for over 25 years. In the last several years, winter peaks on the ERCOT transmission system

have become more significant, with some winter month peaks exceeding summer month peaks in

the same twelve-month period. In addition, the projected substantial increase in large new loads

will increase ERCOT demands in all months of the year. Also, large loads are significant users of

the ERCOT transmission system. However, many existing large loads and many of the new data

center and crypto mining large loads are sophisticated, and capable of self-interrupting or reducing

their energy demands during the ERCOT 4CP periods. As a result, some large loads, commonly

referred to as “free riders,” are able to avoid, or substantially reduce, their charges for transmission
 service. If these large loads self-interrupt during ERCOT’s 4CP periods, this will increase the

allocation of transmission costs to other entities and customers. The use of a 12CP demand

allocation methodology and the 30-minute demand interval will make it more difficult for large

loads to avoid paying for transmission service.

§25.192 (k)(2) Large load customer interconnection fees

       In addition, Houston supports the proposed requirement that transmission service providers

(TSPs) credit their TCOS with amounts received from interconnection fees from large new loads

and from forfeited financial security amounts. These credits to TCOS will reduce ERCOT

transmission rates.

§25.193(d) Large load minimum billing demand

       Houston supports the application of a minimum demand charge for large loads. In addition

to addressing the “free rider” issue, a minimum billing demand provision ensures that the cost of

new or upgraded transmission facilities, such as the Permian Basin Reliability Plant (PBRP)

facilities, are appropriately recovered from the new large loads that cause the need for system

upgrades such as the PBRP. As proposed, the customer’s minimum demand is set as the higher of

their contract demand or their non-coincident peak (NCP) demand. Use of the customer’s contract

demand as one of the factors for determining their minimum billing demand is appropriate for the

following reasons:

       •   The customer’s contract demand is the amount of capacity the TSP must have ready at
           any time to provide service for the customer.

       •   The TSP must plan for transmission facilities necessary to meet customer contract
           demands.

       •   Large customers cause transmission costs based on their contracted demand, as well as
           their NCP demand.

                                                  2
        •   The use of a minimum bill provision using contract demands will help prevent cost
           shifting to other customers.

       •   The use of minimum billing demand provisions provides the TSP with more stable
           revenues.

       In addition to applying the proposed minimum billing demand provision to new large loads,

Houston proposes that it also be applied to existing large loads.

§25.193(d)(2)(B) Large load minimum billing demand

       Houston proposes the following clarifying change to §25.193(d)(2)(B):

       (d)(2)(B) the highest non-coincident peak demand placed by the large load customer on
                 the system in the 12-month period ending with the current month past year;
                 or

                                RESPONSES TO QUESTIONS

       In addition to the comments on the proposed rule, Houston provides responses to

Commission Questions 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6.

1.     Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions
       be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
       different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

       The NCP demand of the large load customer is the customer’s peak demand over a historic

period. The customer’s contract demand should be the highest demand the customer expects to

achieve during the term of the contract. The TSP is obligated to provide transmission service up

to the contract demand. It is the demand that the TSP must plan for and upgrade its transmission

system to provide service for the customer. The minimum demand should be the contract demand

unless the NCP exceeds the contract demand.

2.     Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
          a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
          b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
          c. extended to a longer time period?

                                                 3
        As proposed in Section 25.193(d), minimum billing demand is defined as the higher of

three amounts and, therefore, could increase or decrease from month-to-month. As such, the

minimum billing demand for a large load customer could increase or decrease over time.

Therefore, Houston does not believe it is appropriate to fix the minimum billing demand or to

reduce it periodically over a period. Instead, it may be appropriate to adjust contract demand if

there is a consistent difference (higher or lower) between the initial contract demand and the large

load customer’s monthly NCP demands. This could be an indication that the initial contract

demand was set too low or too high. In that situation, it may be appropriate to allow a revision to

the contract demand.

3.     Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
       lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
       load minimum billing demand:

       a.      reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand
               is some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum
               NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline
               in phases over the years, and how?

       b.      be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large
               load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
               customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
               year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
               weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
               over the years, and how?

       No. Initially, the minimum billing demand should include the actual contract demand factor

as proposed. This is the demand that ERCOT used to develop its annual forecast of peak demands

and the demand level that TSPs typically use to plan for, and construct needed transmission

facilities for large loads. Houston is not opposed to applying a ratchet less than the proposed 100%

ratchet for determining the NCP demand factor in the minimum bill provision in §25.252 of the

proposed rules.
                                                 4
 5.      Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
        transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to
        serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

        Yes, but only for large load-specific or predominantly large load-driven facilities. This

approach is consistent with cost-causation principles and helps ensure that existing customers are

not required to fund transmission investments driven predominantly by new large-load

interconnections.

        The Commission should broaden the definition, but only where the record demonstrates

that:

           1. The transmission project is necessary to accommodate a specific large load request.

           2. The project would not otherwise be required within the planning horizon absent
              that request.

        The benefits are predominantly attributable to the requesting load rather than providing

broad network benefits. Houston proposes the following changes to §25.252(b)(5):

        §25.252 (b)(5) Transmission interconnection costs. All costs associated with the
                       facilities required to physically interconnect or upgrade the
                       interconnection of a transmission-level customer, or a distinct set of
                       transmission-level customers, to the existing transmission network,
                       including interconnection lines, substation additions or modifications, and
                       associated equipment necessary to establish or modify service, including
                       transmission projects identified through an ERCOT batch study that
                       are primarily attributable to serving the transmission capacity
                       requirements of a large load customer or discrete group of large load
                       customers.

6.      If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of
        whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity,
        how should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments
        and transmission planning studies?

        The Commission should distinguish between transmission planning and resource adequacy

functions. Transmission facilities must be planned to serve reserved capacity because the system

                                                5
 must be capable of delivering the service that has been contracted and funded. However, resource

adequacy assessments should avoid assuming that all reserved transmission capacity represents

contemporaneous energy consumption. Accordingly, reserved capacity should be modeled as

committed load for transmission planning purposes but should be separately identified and forecast

using reasonable energization assumptions for resource adequacy purposes. The Commission

should also clarify that transmission facilities identified through ERCOT batch studies are

transmission interconnection costs when the facilities are primarily required to accommodate the

transmission capacity needs of a specific large load customer or discrete group of large load

customers and would not otherwise be required absent those load requests. Houston proposes

adding §25.252(d)(3):

       §252(d)(3) Treatment of Reserved Transmission Capacity.

                    (A) For transmission planning studies, a large load customer that has
                        executed an interconnection agreement and satisfied applicable
                        financial commitment requirements under §25.194 of this title shall
                        be modeled as load at the level of reserved transmission capacity
                        made available to serve that customer.

                    (B) For resource adequacy reports, forecasts, and assessments, ERCOT
                        shall separately identify reserved but unenergized transmission
                        capacity from actual load and may utilize energization status,
                        demonstrated development milestones, historical utilization, or
                        other reasonable forecasting methodologies in estimating expected
                        load consumption.

                    (C) Nothing in this subsection shall require reserved but unenergized
                        transmission capacity to be treated as actual load for purposes of
                        resource adequacy assessments.

CITY OF HOUSTON, TEXAS

                      CITY OF HOUSTON’S INITIAL COMMENTS

                                     Executive Summary

Houston submits the following substantive recommendations in the comments above:

1.     Houston supports the proposed change to a 12CP demand allocation methodology for
       determining transmission service rates.

2.     Houston supports the use of a minimum billing demand provision for new large loads, as
       proposed in the rule.

3.     Houston also proposes that the proposed minimum bill be implemented for existing large
       loads, not just new large loads. Currently, large loads are able to self-interrupt during
       ERCOT CP periods and avoid, or substantially reduce, charges for ERCOT transmission
       system service. The use of a minimum bill provision will ensure that existing large loads
       also pay for a portion of the transmission service they receive.

4.     Houston supports the proposed requirement that TSPs credit their transmission cost of
       service (TCOS) with amounts received from interconnection fees from large new loads and
       from forfeited financial security amounts.

5.     The Commission should clarify that transmission interconnection costs include
       transmission facilities or upgrades identified through an ERCOT batch study when those
       facilities are primarily required to serve the transmission capacity needs of a specific or
       discrete group of large load customers and would not otherwise be required absent those
       load requests. This approach is consistent with cost-causation principles and helps ensure
       that existing customers are not required to fund transmission investments driven
       predominantly by new large-load interconnections.

6.     Reserved transmission capacity should be treated as committed load for transmission
       planning purposes because the transmission system must be capable of serving the capacity
       that has been reserved through an executed interconnection agreement. However, for
       resource adequacy reports and assessments, ERCOT should separately identify reserved
       but unenergized load and apply reasonable forecasting assumptions, rather than treating all
       reserved capacity as actual load. This approach supports prudent transmission planning
       while avoiding overstatement of near-term demand in resource adequacy evaluations.
